title: Fluency, Accuracy, Complexity

pts: Fluency: producing language at a natural pace with few unnatural pauses.
Accuracy: producing language that conforms to target-language norms.
Complexity: using a wider range of, and more sophisticated, language forms.

v: Two one-minute recordings of learners speaking

items: Record two learners (with consent) each talking for one minute about a festival.
Listen once for fluency: count long or unnatural pauses and restarts.
Listen again for accuracy: count clauses with and without errors.
Listen a third time for complexity: note connectors (because, when, although) and less common words.
Compare the two learners and discuss with a colleague.
In a training session, rate the same recording in three groups, one per dimension, and compare.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Fluency: speech rate, number and length of pauses, false starts.
Complexity: subordinate clauses, variety of verb forms, range of vocabulary.

blocks.x: A transcript extract (written for this book):

lines: For Pongal we are… we are making sweet pongal, and my grandmother, she tells the story of the cows, because it is the day for thanking them.

blocks.x: Pauses and a restart (fluency), one error in we are making for a habit (accuracy), and a because clause with a relative idea (complexity).

body: Purpose: to define the three dimensions. Content: a speech bubble viewed through three coloured lenses: a stopwatch lens (‘Fluency: pace and flow’), a tick lens (‘Accuracy: correct forms’) and a staircase lens (‘Complexity: range and sophistication’). Style: clean infographic. Board version: three circles labelled F, A and C.

items: Google Docs voice typing (free, in the Chrome browser) for a rough first transcript.

blocks.x: A phone’s voice recorder and a notebook tally.

pts: Working memory and attention are limited; pushing harder on one dimension often draws resource away from another.
A task that maximises fluency (talk fast, don't stop) predictably costs some accuracy.
This is a resource trade-off, not a sign of inconsistent ability.

items: Pairs tell a picture story to each other in one minute (fluency pressure).
Pairs tell it again with a new instruction: every verb in the past tense must be correct, with no time limit.
Then a third time: use at least two when or because sentences.
Ask: what happened to your speed? To your mistakes? To your sentences?
Draw the juggler on the board and explain limited attention.
Teachers try it in a language they are learning.
Support: a four-picture story with key verbs.
Challenge: a six-picture story with an unexpected ending.

lines: S1: When I was fast, I forgot the past tense.
S2: When I thought about ‘because’, I stopped many times.
T: Yes. Your brain has only so much attention. Today it went to speed; then to correctness; then to longer sentences.

blocks.x: Working memory and attention are limited; pushing on one dimension often draws resources from another (Skehan 1998). This is a resource trade-off, not a sign of inconsistent ability.

body: Purpose: to show competition for attention. Content: a learner juggling three balls labelled F, A and C, with a thought bubble showing a small tank marked ‘attention’; when one ball rises high, the others dip. Style: playful, simple. Board version: a stick figure with three circles.

items: Classroomscreen (free basic plan) for a visible one-minute timer.

blocks.x: The teacher counts down on a wall clock.

body: Not all researchers agree that the three dimensions must compete. Robinson’s Cognition Hypothesis predicts that some cognitively demanding tasks can raise accuracy and complexity together (Robinson 2001). For classroom planning, the useful point is the same: task design shapes the language produced.

pts: Time pressure, familiar topics, and low-stakes framing push output toward fluency.
Fluency tasks should minimise interruption and correction, protecting the communicative flow (Unit 8's delayed correction).
Repetition of a similar task type across a course reliably increases fluency over time.

items: Learners choose a familiar topic (my village, my favourite food, a journey).
Learners stand or face in two lines. Speaker A talks to Partner 1 for four minutes.
A moves to a new partner and tells the same content in three minutes.
A moves again and tells it in two minutes.
Swap roles and repeat with B as the speaker.
For young or lower-level learners, use 2/1.5/1 minutes.
On fixed benches, speakers turn to the left, the right and then behind.
Support: three picture prompts or keywords on a card.
Challenge: add one new detail each time while keeping to time.

blocks.x: A learner’s three versions (written for this book):

lines: 4 minutes: Last summer we went to… to Madurai. We went by, by train. It was… very long journey…
2 minutes: Last summer we took the train to Madurai. It was a long journey, but we saw the temple…

blocks.x: Repetition with a new listener and less time pushes learners to speak more smoothly (Nation 1989; Arevart and Nation 1991). Fluency tasks use familiar topics, time pressure and low stakes, and they minimize correction (Unit 8).

body: Purpose: to show the 4/3/2 technique. Content: three pairs of learners in sequence under clocks showing four, three and two minutes; the speech bubble grows smoother from left to right. Style: clear sequence. Board version: three clocks and arrows.

items: Online Stopwatch (free, with advertising) for a large countdown on a projector.

blocks.x: The teacher calls ‘Change!’ using a watch.

pts: Reduced time pressure, familiar and narrow language, and an audience raise attention to accuracy.
Planning time before a task, as in Unit 28's task cycle, is one of the most reliable accuracy boosts available.
Explicit accuracy focus is more appropriate immediately before or after a task than during its live communicative phase.

v: A narrative picture sequence; planning sheets

items: Show a six-picture story about a lost puppy.
Give ten minutes of individual planning with a sheet (notes only, not full sentences).
Allow notes in English or the home language.
Learners tell the story to a partner without a time limit, taking time to choose words.
Finally, learners tell it to a new partner who will retell it to the class.
Guided planning: add one question to the sheet, such as Which past tense verbs will you need?
Support: a planning sheet with boxes for each picture.
Challenge: tell the story from the puppy’s point of view.

blocks.x: A planning sheet (written for this book):

lines: Picture 1: Riya – park – puppy – ran away. Picture 2: searched – asked vendor – ‘not seen’. Useful words: searched, noticed, suddenly, finally.

blocks.x: Pre-task planning tends to raise fluency and complexity, with more variable effects on accuracy (Foster and Skehan 1996). Giving learners time to speak without pressure, so that they can monitor while speaking, appears to help accuracy more directly (Yuan and Ellis 2003). An audience also raises attention to accuracy, as in the report stage of Unit 28.

body: Purpose: to show planning before performance. Content: a learner with short notes, some in Kannada script, then the same learner speaking calmly to a partner. Style: calm, two-panel. Board version: a notebook and a speech bubble.

items: Vocaroo (free) for learners to record and listen to their own story.

pts: Unfamiliar topics, more cognitively demanding tasks, and reduced time pressure encourage more complex language attempts.
Complexity gains often come at a temporary cost to fluency, as new forms are used more tentatively.
Complexity-focused tasks work best when accuracy demands are simultaneously relaxed.

v: A short problem card; frames for complex sentences

items: Give groups a problem card: the town has too much plastic waste; the council must choose one solution.
Groups discuss three options and their consequences.
Display frames for complex sentences (see model language).
Groups present their recommendation with reasons and conditions.
Tell learners that errors will not be marked in this task; ambition will.
Use a topic from a science or social studies chapter, such as floods or water sharing.
Support: two options instead of three.
Challenge: each group must answer a counter-argument.

lines: If the council…, then… / Although…, we think… / The problem is not only…, but also… / We would recommend… because…
Although the plastic ban is difficult for shopkeepers, we think if the council gives cloth bags free, people will follow.

blocks.x: Unfamiliar topics, reasoning, and reduced time pressure encourage more complex language (Skehan 1998). Gains in complexity often cost some fluency, as new forms are used tentatively, so relax accuracy demands for this task.

body: Purpose: to show complexity as reaching for new forms. Content: a learner reaching up a bookshelf for words labelled although, if…then, not only…but also; a sign below says ‘Mistakes allowed today’. Style: encouraging. Board version: a shelf with three phrases.

items: Padlet (free plan) for groups to post their recommendation.

blocks.x: Chart paper for each group’s recommendation.

pts: No single task optimises all three dimensions simultaneously — sequence different task types across a course instead.
A course entirely of fluency tasks under-develops accuracy and complexity, and vice versa.
This connects directly to Unit 11's unit-level pacing — plan the trilogy's balance at the unit level, not just per lesson.

items: List every speaking and writing task in a two-week plan.
Mark each task F, A or C according to what it mainly pushes.
Look for imbalance: all accuracy, or no complexity.
Replace or adjust one or two tasks to restore balance.
Build in one repeated task: the same type done again a week later.
A school English department maps a whole term together.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A fortnight before and after (written for this book):

lines: Before: A A A F A A A A (eight tasks, almost all accuracy).
After: F A C A F A C F (repetition of the 4/3/2 task in weeks one and two).

blocks.x: No single task optimizes all three dimensions. A course made only of fluency tasks under-develops accuracy and complexity, and the reverse. Repeating a similar task after an interval tends to improve performance (Bygate 2001). Plan the balance at unit level (Unit 11), not only lesson by lesson.

body: Purpose: to show sequencing. Content: a two-week calendar with each task coloured by dimension (blue F, green A, orange C) and a small balance scale beside it. Style: planner-like. Board version: a row of letters.

items: Google Sheets (free) with coloured cells for a term map.

points.h: Reading the Trilogy in Learner Output
pts: A burst of errors during a fast, fluent stretch may reflect a fluency-focused task working as intended, not regression.
Compare output across different task types before concluding a learner has an accuracy problem in general.
This reframes error patterns as partly a function of task design, not purely of underlying competence.

v: Two samples from one learner on different task types

items: Collect two samples from one learner: one from a fluency task, one from a planned accuracy task.
Count errors per ten clauses in each.
Note the difference, and what the task asked for.
Before writing a report comment, ask whether the pattern reflects the task or the learner.
Write one comment that names both.
Compare the same learner’s speaking and writing on the same topic.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Two samples from one learner (written for this book):

lines: 4/3/2 task: 7 errors in 10 clauses, fast and confident.
Planned story: 2 errors in 10 clauses, slower, with two when clauses.
Arjun speaks confidently and fast. When he has time to plan, his accuracy is good. Next step: keep accuracy when speaking faster.

blocks.x: A burst of errors in a fast, fluent stretch may mean a fluency task is working, not that the learner has regressed. Compare output across task types before concluding that a learner has an accuracy problem in general.

body: Purpose: to show variation across tasks. Content: the same learner twice, mid-conversation (‘fast, more errors’) and at a desk (‘planned, fewer errors’), captioned ‘same learner, different task’. Style: realistic. Board version: two boxes with numbers.

items: Google Forms (free) for a simple sample log per learner.

blocks.x: A learner record page with samples stapled in.

body: Keep one short speaking sample per learner per term, recorded on a phone. With forty learners that is forty minutes of listening a term, and it gives far better evidence than memory.

pts: Ask which dimension this specific task is meant to prioritise, before choosing time pressure, topic familiarity, and correction policy.
Mismatched expectations — wanting accuracy from a fluency task — are a common source of frustration for both teacher and learner.
State the dimension explicitly to learners too; performance calibrates once they know what's being prioritised.

items: Before choosing time limits, topic and correction policy, decide which dimension the task is for.
Make three cards: Speak smoothly, Speak correctly, Try something new.
Show the relevant card before each task and explain it in one sentence.
Match the feedback to the card afterwards.
Learners choose their own personal focus card for a repeated task.
Support: pictures on the cards (a running figure, a tick, a staircase).
Challenge: learners set a numerical target, such as fewer than three long pauses.

lines: Which dimension? → Time limit? → Familiar or new topic? → Planning time? → Correction during, after, or not at all?
T: This task is ‘Speak smoothly’. Don’t stop to correct yourselves. I’ll listen, but I won’t correct now.

blocks.x: Mismatched expectations, such as wanting accuracy from a fluency task, frustrate both teacher and learner. Once learners know what is being prioritized, their performance usually adjusts.

body: Purpose: to show the focus cards. Content: three cards on the board with icons: a runner (‘Speak smoothly’), a tick (‘Speak correctly’) and a staircase (‘Try something new’). Style: bold, poster-like. Board version: three hand-drawn cards.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for printable focus cards.

blocks.x: Three hand-made cards reused every lesson.

body: For one week, show a focus card before every speaking task and match your feedback to it. Keep a note of how many learners speak in fluency tasks when they know they will not be corrected.

dek: Unit 29 of 100: a learner's limited attention has to be shared between speaking fluently, accurately, and with complexity — task design decides where that attention goes.

aims.x: This unit looks closely at three qualities of learner language: fluency, accuracy and complexity. Because attention is limited, learners cannot maximize all three at once, and the way a task is designed decides where their attention goes. The unit shows how to push deliberately towards each dimension, how to balance them across a course, and how to read learner output with the trilogy in mind.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: define fluency, accuracy and complexity and describe simple classroom measures of each;
explain why the three dimensions compete for attention;
design tasks that push towards fluency, towards accuracy or towards complexity;
use planning time and task repetition deliberately;
balance the three dimensions across a unit of work;
interpret learners’ errors partly as a result of task design;
tell learners which dimension a task prioritizes.

why: Why this matters. Without understanding this trilogy, a teacher can mistake a fluency task's errors for failure, or an accuracy task's hesitance for lack of ability.

background.x: Christopher Brumfit (1984) drew a now-familiar distinction between fluency activities, where learners use language naturally for meaning, and accuracy activities, where attention is on correct form. Peter Skehan (1998) added a third dimension, complexity: the range and sophistication of language a learner attempts. He argued that learners have a limited capacity for attention, so that under pressure they must prioritize. A learner speaking fast about a familiar topic may be fluent but make errors; one attempting new structures may slow down and hesitate. Researchers now often speak of CAF: complexity, accuracy and fluency (Housen and Kuiken 2009).

Not everyone accepts the trade-off view. Peter Robinson (2001) proposed the Cognition Hypothesis, which predicts that more cognitively demanding tasks can push accuracy and complexity up together, at least in some conditions. The research evidence is mixed, and the debate continues. For teachers, however, both positions lead to the same practical conclusion: task features such as planning time, familiarity, structure and cognitive demand change the kind of language learners produce. Research on pre-task planning (Foster and Skehan 1996; Ellis 2005), on unpressured on-line planning (Yuan and Ellis 2003) and on task repetition (Bygate 2001) gives teachers usable levers.

In many Indian classrooms the balance is tilted heavily towards accuracy. Written examinations reward correct forms; speaking is rarely assessed; and learners often feel that a sentence with an error should not be said at all. The NEP 2020 and NCF 2023 emphasize competencies and the ability to use language, not only knowledge about it (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020; NCERT 2023). Planning deliberately for all three dimensions is one practical response. Home languages have a role too: planning notes in Kannada or Hindi can free attention for fluent English performance.

items: CAF profile. Rate one recorded sample per learner on three simple scales each term.
Repetition gain. Compare the first and third versions of a 4/3/2 talk for pauses and speed.
Planned performance. Assess a planned story for accuracy and complexity with a short rubric.
Task log. Review your own task log each month for balance across the three dimensions.
Which dimension do your lessons push most, and which least?
How do you react to errors in fluency tasks?
Do your learners know what each speaking task is for?
How often do your learners repeat a task?
How might planning in the home language help your learners speak more fluently in English?
What evidence do you use when you write that a learner ‘makes many mistakes’?

Bygate, M. 2001. ‘Effects of task repetition on the structure and control of oral language’ in M. Bygate, P. Skehan, and M. Swain (eds.). Researching Pedagogic Tasks. Harlow: Longman.
Ellis, R. (ed.). 2005. Planning and Task Performance in a Second Language. Amsterdam: John Benjamins.
Foster, P. and P. Skehan. 1996. ‘The influence of planning and task type on second language performance’. Studies in Second Language Acquisition 18/3: 299–323.
Housen, A. and F. Kuiken. 2009. ‘Complexity, accuracy, and fluency in second language acquisition’. Applied Linguistics 30/4: 461–73.
Robinson, P. 2001. ‘Task complexity, task difficulty, and task production: exploring interactions in a componential framework’. Applied Linguistics 22/1: 27–57.

terms.def: A fluency activity in which a learner gives the same talk three times to different listeners in four, three and then two minutes, so that repetition and time pressure make speech smoother (Nation 1989).

The extent to which a learner’s language is free from errors in grammar, vocabulary and pronunciation; one of the three dimensions of performance, with complexity and fluency, that teachers balance in task design.
Robinson’s (2001) proposal that more cognitively demanding tasks can increase accuracy and complexity together, rather than forcing a trade-off between them.
The range and sophistication of the language a learner uses, such as varied vocabulary and subordinate clauses; one of three dimensions of performance, with accuracy and fluency.
A three-part framework for describing learner performance, often abbreviated CAF, used in research and for assessing speaking and writing (Housen and Kuiken 2009).
The ability to speak or write at a natural speed with limited hesitation, focusing on meaning. It is often balanced against accuracy and complexity in planning tasks and giving feedback.

The idea that learners can attend to only so much at once, so that focusing on fluency, accuracy or complexity may come at the expense of the others (Skehan 1998); planning time and task repetition can ease this pressure.
Planning that speakers do while performing a task, adjusting and monitoring their speech as they go, especially when there is no time pressure.
Time given before a task for learners to plan the content and language of their performance; research suggests it tends to increase fluency and complexity, with more mixed effects on accuracy.
Asking learners to do the same or a similar task again, often with a different partner, so that freed attention can go to fluency, accuracy or complexity (Bygate 2001).
